title: Small job shops lose work because RFQ quoting from PDF prints is slow and backlogs when demand rises
affected_user: Owner / estimator at a 5-50 person CNC machining or custom tooling job shop
job_to_be_done: Turn an emailed RFQ package (PDF drawings, sometimes STEP files, often multi-part) into a priced, accurate quote fast enough to win the job without under-pricing it
current_process: Estimator opens each PDF print, reads tolerances/threads/notes (often missing from 3D CAD), estimates setups, cycle time, material and outside processes by hand or in a spreadsheet/ERP quote module, then emails a quote back; multi-part packages get triaged or deprioritized when odds look low
what_fails: Quote turnaround stretches to days; buyers order from the first responder; when RFQ volume rises the internal quoting step becomes a backlog and strike rate falls; detailed quoting consumes a large chunk of the owner's week
failure_frequency: Per-shop win rates reported on Practical Machinist range from 5-10% with new prospects to ~50% with established customers; one owner reported strike rate falling from ~50% to ~25% when daily quote volume rose from ~1 to ~8 (forum anecdotes, undated/older)
cost_of_failure: Lost jobs ordered elsewhere before quote arrives (buyer anecdote: RFQ to six shops, ordered from first two responders within a day); owner labor on quoting. Vendor claim (Paperless Parts, unverified): quotes sent within 24h win ~2x as often as those after 48h
existing_workaround: Triage RFQs and only quote high-probability ones; 5-minute rule-of-thumb quotes accepting some losses; stop quoting customers with <25% win rate; adopt cloud quoting tools (Paperless Parts) or marketplaces (Xometry) for simple parts
who_pays_today: Shop owner/estimator time; subscriptions to Paperless Parts, ProShop, JobBOSS quote modules; Xometry/marketplace fee spread

sources.note: Shop owners describe RFQ backlog when quoting process takes too long internally and share triage strategies.
Buyer reports ordering from first responders before other quotes arrive; shops say slow quotes lose work.
Owners report quote win rates and one describes win rate halving as quote volume increased.
Recent (~9 months old) thread on how to quickly extract dimensions from RFQ prints; PDFs needed because CAD lacks tolerances/threads.
Modern Machine Shop/Paperless Parts case study claiming 6x faster quoting after switching tools (vendor-adjacent).
Summarizes forum-reported win rates (5-10% new prospects, ~50% repeat) and vendor 24h-vs-48h claim.

firsthand_evidence: A Practical Machinist poster said shops start losing work because it takes too long to get the quote in; a buyer described sending an RFQ to about six shops, getting two replies within a day, and ordering before the rest arrived. Another owner reported his strike rate dropped from roughly half to a quarter once he went from about one quote a day to eight.
key_unknowns: No primary statistic on median quote turnaround or quoting hours per week for small shops; forum threads are mostly older than 2025; unclear what fraction of shops already use Paperless Parts-class tools; no 2026 r/Machinists threads surfaced (search budget exhausted).
technical_unlock: Vision-capable LLMs can now read PDF drawings (GD&T, threads, notes) and STEP geometry to pre-extract features and tolerance-driven cost drivers; combined with a shop's historical quote/job data this makes a first-pass quote draft feasible for a solo developer without CAD-kernel licensing.
why_now: Multimodal models reading engineering prints became usable in 2025-2026; reshoring/tariff-driven RFQ volume increases at domestic shops amplify quoting backlogs (inferred).
existing_solutions: Paperless Parts, ProShop ERP, JobBOSS2, Xometry/Protolabs instant quoting (for simple geometry), CostIt, aPriori (enterprise)

title: Small DoD subcontractors face six-figure CMMC compliance costs, long C3PAO queues, and policy whiplash after the July 2026 Phase II suspension
affected_user: Owner / IT-compliance lead at a 10-100 employee machine shop, electronics or fabrication subcontractor handling CUI under DFARS 252.204-7012/7021
job_to_be_done: Stay eligible for DoD prime flow-down contracts by meeting NIST SP 800-171 / CMMC Level 1-2 requirements, documenting an SSP/POA&M, posting SPRS scores, and (when required) passing a third-party assessment
current_process: Hire an MSP/consultant to build an SSP and POA&M, buy GCC High or enclave tooling, self-assess and submit SPRS score, and queue for a C3PAO assessment; primes flow down requirements but the sub bears the cost
what_fails: Costs are far beyond small-shop budgets (SBA estimate up to ~$593,800 per certification for third-party assessment, ~$388,600 for self-assessment); C3PAO scheduling lead times of 6-12 months; on July 13, 2026 DoW suspended Phase II (which was due Nov 10, 2026) and launched a 60-day review, leaving shops that had already spent money unsure whether their investment was needed, while Phase I self-assessment and 800-171 obligations still apply
failure_frequency: Affects every DIB subcontractor handling CUI; NDIA (Feb 2024 comment) and SBA Office of Advocacy flagged SMB burden; DoD OSBP ran a Nov 2025 pulse survey on small-business CMMC readiness
cost_of_failure: Consultant estimates $34k-$112k implementation plus $30k-$60k assessment and $10k-$30k/yr maintenance (vendor guides); SBA figure up to $593,800 per certification; loss of contract eligibility if non-compliant; sunk prep cost if Phase II is cancelled
existing_workaround: Enclave products (PreVeil, GCC High), MSP compliance packages, delaying investment pending the review, exiting DoD work, relying on existing Level 2 (C3PAO) certs which remain valid
who_pays_today: Subcontractors pay consultants, MSPs, enclave vendors, C3PAOs; primes absorb supplier-attrition cost; DoD pays via higher prices

sources.note: SBA cites compliance cost up to ~$593,800 per certification (C3PAO) and ~$388,600 (self) and commends Phase II suspension.
DoW announcement suspending Phase II and creating a CMMC Reform Task Force for a 60-day review; Phase I and NIST 800-171 obligations remain.
News coverage of the suspension and program review.
CSIS analysis of the pause's effect on the defense industrial base.
48 CFR rule published Sept 10, 2025, effective Nov 10, 2025 (Phase 1 start).
Third-party estimate of C3PAO lead times 3-12 months, possibly 24-30 months by late 2026 (unverified).
Vendor cost ranges ($34k-$112k implementation; $30k-$60k assessment) and note that no small-business exemption exists.
NDIA public comment arguing CMMC 2.0 increases cost and scope beyond current contractual requirements, especially for SMBs.

firsthand_evidence: No individual shop-owner post was captured (search budget exhausted before Reddit/forum queries ran). Institutional voices: NDIA's public comment says CMMC 2.0 raises cost and scope beyond current contractual requirements and names small and medium businesses as most affected; SBA Advocacy raised the same concerns and endorsed the suspension.
key_unknowns: Outcome of the 60-day task force review (expected ~mid-Sept 2026) was not found; actual number of small subs that have dropped DoD work; real C3PAO queue length (official figures not found); whether Level 2 (Self) will become the long-term norm, which would shift the pain from assessment to self-documentation.
technical_unlock: LLM-assisted SSP/POA&M drafting and evidence mapping against the 110 NIST 800-171 controls is feasible, but the hard cost is enclave infrastructure and the assessment itself, not documents; a solo developer can address the documentation/self-assessment slice only.
why_now: 48 CFR rule took effect Nov 10, 2025; Phase II suspended July 13, 2026 pending reform; shops are in limbo between Phase I self-assessment obligations and an uncertain Phase II.
existing_solutions: PreVeil, Summit 7, Microsoft GCC High, Secureframe, Vanta, Drata, FutureFeed, dozens of MSP/consultant packages, C3PAOs

title: End of de minimis forces small importers into formal/informal entries with 10-digit HTS codes, bonds, MPF and broker fees on every low-value shipment
affected_user: Small e-commerce brand, hobby-parts seller, or SMB manufacturer importing components/finished goods in shipments under $800 (previously duty- and entry-free)
job_to_be_done: Get low-value international shipments cleared through CBP correctly and cheaply, with the right HTS classification, country-of-origin and stacked tariff rates
current_process: Shipments that previously cleared under Section 321 with no entry now require an informal or formal entry with a 10-digit HTS code, declared value, duty payment, a customs bond for formal entries, and usually a licensed broker; postal shipments have separate new entry requirements
what_fails: Per-shipment broker/entry fees and MPF (FY2026: 0.3464% ad valorem, min $33.58, max $651.50 per formal entry) can exceed the goods' value; importers unfamiliar with HTS must classify every SKU; misclassification exposes them to penalties; brokers report structural workload and liability increases; timelines were confusing (China/HK May 2, 2025; global Aug 29, 2025; CBP indefinite suspension notice June 24, 2026; statutory repeal via OBBBA effective July 1, 2027)
failure_frequency: Every sub-$800 shipment from every small importer since Aug 29, 2025 (all modes other than postal network subject to CBP's June 2026 indefinite suspension)
cost_of_failure: Broker fees plus MPF plus duty on each entry; one financial advisor piece (Apr 2026) describes small businesses coping by consolidating orders or absorbing margins; specific small-importer dollar figures were not found
existing_workaround: Consolidate orders into bulk shipments; self-file through ACE; move inventory to US 3PLs; raise prices; drop low-margin SKUs; use carriers' DDP services at a premium
who_pays_today: Small importers pay customs brokers (per-entry fees), carriers' brokerage surcharges, duties and MPF; brokers hire staff for volume

sources.note: CBP Federal Register notice indefinitely suspending de minimis for all non-postal modes; requires informal or formal entry.
BDO summary of suspension and new postal entry requirements.
Describes bond requirement for formal entries and FY2026 MPF rate (0.3464%, $33.58 min / $651.50 max).
Broker-side view: structural increase in workload, liability exposure and client-service complexity.
Advisor article on how small businesses are coping with de minimis ending.
Importer guide listing 10-digit HTS, declared value, duty payment now required on each shipment; notes OBBBA statutory repeal effective July 1, 2027.

firsthand_evidence: No Reddit/forum first-person post was captured before the search budget ran out; evidence is regulatory notices and broker/advisor commentary. Brokers themselves describe the change as a structural increase in workload and liability.
key_unknowns: Actual per-entry broker fee ranges small importers pay in 2026; how many small importers quit importing; share who self-file in ACE; whether HTS misclassification penalties against small importers have actually risen (CBP enforcement data not found).
technical_unlock: LLM-based HTS classification with retrieval over the current HTSUS and CBP CROSS rulings, plus automated tariff-stacking (Section 232/301/122/reciprocal) rate lookup, can give small importers a defensible pre-classification before they pay a broker; ACE self-filing APIs exist.
why_now: De minimis suspended globally Aug 29, 2025 and indefinitely by CBP June 24, 2026; statutory repeal July 1, 2027; tariff-rate stacking changed repeatedly in 2025-2026.
existing_solutions: Customs brokers (Flexport, UPS/FedEx brokerage), Avalara Cross-Border, Zonos, tariff lookup tools (tariffstool.com), CBP ACE self-filing

title: Small importers struggle to recover IEEPA tariff refunds: ACH/4811 paperwork holds, phased CAPE eligibility, and finally-liquidated entries requiring a CIT lawsuit
affected_user: Small-to-mid importer of record (manufacturers importing components, e-commerce brands) that paid IEEPA tariffs in 2025-2026
job_to_be_done: Identify every entry on which IEEPA duties were paid, determine liquidation status, and file the correct refund claim in CBP's CAPE/ACE system to get money back with interest
current_process: After the Supreme Court held (Feb 20, 2026) that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, CBP began refunds via CAPE on Apr 20, 2026 in phases: Phase 1 unliquidated entries and entries no more than 80 days past liquidation; Phase 2 (June 29) reconciliation entries; Phase 3 (Oct 6, 2026) entries liquidated more than 80 days, but only for importers who are plaintiffs with a pending CIT case; refunds go only to the importer of record or a CBP Form 4811 notify party, by ACH
what_fails: As of Oct 2, 2026 about 20,362 refunds worth ~$1.1B were on hold because importers had not provided ACH bank details; non-litigating importers with finally liquidated entries may need to file suit; the government appealed the portion of the order covering them; Section 122 surcharge refunds had no route as of Sept 25, 2026; refunds are not automatic and require ACE filings small importers rarely do themselves
failure_frequency: One-time but enormous: ~$136.6B in refund claims accepted as of Oct 2, 2026 (CBP via Thompson Hine); every importer that paid IEEPA duties is affected
cost_of_failure: Unrecovered duties (potentially thousands to millions per importer) plus interest; broker/law-firm fees to file; 20,362 refunds (~$1.1B) stuck on missing ACH enrollment alone
existing_workaround: Hire customs brokers or trade law firms to file CAPE claims and protests; file a CIT suit to preserve rights on finally liquidated entries; UPS and other brokers offer refund-filing services
who_pays_today: Importers pay brokers/law firms contingency or hourly fees; CBP staff process claims; Treasury pays interest

sources.note: Law firm confirms Phase 3 launch Oct 6, 2026, limited to importers with pending CIT cases.
Describes Phase 2 (reconciliation entries) and the phased CAPE structure.
Reports Supreme Court ruling Feb 20, 2026 and CAPE refunds starting Apr 20, 2026; cites ~$136.6B accepted claims and 20,362 refunds (~$1.1B) on hold for missing ACH details as of Oct 2.
Importers with finally liquidated entries may need to file suit; government appealed that portion of the order.
CPA-firm FAQ: refunds only to importer of record or Form 4811 notify party; not automatic; ACE filing required.
Carrier brokerage markets a paid refund-filing service, indicating importers cannot easily self-serve.

firsthand_evidence: No individual importer post captured. The strongest signal is CBP's own figure (reported by Avalara/Thompson Hine) that over 20,000 refunds worth about $1.1B sat on hold purely because importers had not completed ACH enrollment, a paperwork failure rather than a legal one.
key_unknowns: Distribution of refund size among small importers; how many small importers have unclaimed refunds on finally liquidated entries; outcome of the government's appeal; whether CBP will open a non-litigant path for Phase 3; exact date consistency (some sources give CIT directive Mar 4, 2026).
technical_unlock: ACE entry-summary data exports plus a rules engine for liquidation-status/phase eligibility can tell a small importer exactly which entries qualify and generate the ACH/4811 and CAPE submission package; this is data plumbing, not research.
why_now: Supreme Court IEEPA ruling Feb 20, 2026; CAPE phases Apr 20, June 29 and Oct 6, 2026; appeal pending on finally liquidated entries; time-limited window.
existing_solutions: Customs brokers (UPS, Flexport), trade law firms, Avalara, CLA and other accounting firms offering refund services

title: AS9102 first-article inspection reports take a day or more per part and get held up for weeks by sub-tier certs and prime-specific checklists
affected_user: Quality manager / inspector at a 10-100 person aerospace or defense machining supplier shipping to Lockheed, Boeing, RTX and their tier-1s
job_to_be_done: Produce a complete, customer-accepted AS9102 Rev C FAI package (Forms 1-3, ballooned drawing, material/special-process certs) before first shipment on every new part or revision
current_process: Manually balloon every characteristic on the drawing, measure each, transcribe results into Forms 1-3 (Excel or customer-mandated templates), collect material certs and special-process (plating, heat treat, NDT) certificates from sub-tier suppliers, add prime-specific checklists (e.g. Lockheed SQAG 001 Issue 6, Feb 2026, requires LM supplier-quality approval before any shipment)
what_fails: Complex parts with 200+ characteristics take 8-24+ engineering hours; a missing special-process cert or an unordered supplier package stalls the FAIR for weeks; each prime's checklist differs; Rev C removed signature fields but did not shrink documentation burden; rejected FAIRs delay first shipment and revenue
failure_frequency: Every new part number, every drawing revision, and every lapse >2 years in production (AS9102 triggers); per-shop frequency unknown
cost_of_failure: 8-24+ hours of QA/engineering time per complex FAIR (vendor estimates, unverified); weeks of shipment delay when sub-tier paperwork is missing; cost of FAIR software seats
existing_workaround: Excel templates with macros; buy ballooning/FAI software (InspectionXpert, Ideagen, Connect981, High QA, DISCUS); hire contract inspectors; pre-order sub-tier cert packages with the PO
who_pays_today: Supplier QA payroll; FAI software vendors; primes' supplier-quality engineers who review and reject packages

sources.note: Lockheed Martin UK FAI guidebook Issue 6 (Feb 2026): FAIR must be reviewed and approved by LMUK supplier quality before any material shipment; prime-specific additions beyond AS9102 forms.
Vendor estimates complex FAIR with 200+ characteristics at 8-24+ engineering hours.
Vendor says manual FAIR can take a full day per part; claims automated ballooning reduces to under 2 hours.
Notes that chasing a missing special-process certificate or unordered supplier package can take weeks; calendar delay is paperwork, not measurement.
Tier-1 (LMI Aerospace) FAI guideline Rev L showing customer-specific FAIR requirements layered on AS9102.
Vendor description of Forms 1-3 and ballooning burden; documentation burden did not shrink with Rev C.

firsthand_evidence: No forum post captured (planned r/Machinists AS9102 query was blocked by the search budget). Evidence is prime documents and vendor commentary; the prime documents independently confirm that each customer layers its own FAI checklist and approval gate on top of AS9102.
key_unknowns: Independent survey of FAIR hours or rejection rates at small suppliers; share of small shops still using Excel vs. FAI software; how much of the delay is sub-tier cert chasing vs. ballooning; whether primes accept AI-generated ballooning.
technical_unlock: Vision models can balloon PDF/DXF drawings and map characteristics to AS9102 Form 3 rows; LLM extraction can read material and process certs to auto-populate Form 2 and flag missing sub-tier documents before the part is finished.
why_now: Prime guidebooks keep revising (Lockheed SQAG 001 Issue 6, Feb 2026); aerospace ramp-up (reshored defense work) increases new-part FAIRs at small suppliers (inferred).
existing_solutions: InspectionXpert (Ideagen), High QA, DISCUS, Connect981, QA-CAD, Net-Inspect, ProShop ERP FAI module

title: Construction subcontractor pay applications get bounced for lien-waiver, certified-payroll and compliance-document gaps, delaying payment
affected_user: Office manager / controller at a small-to-mid trade subcontractor (electrical, mechanical, concrete) billing GCs monthly, especially on prevailing-wage (Davis-Bacon) jobs
job_to_be_done: Submit a monthly pay application (AIA G702/G703-style schedule of values) with conditional and unconditional lien waivers, certified payroll (WH-347) on prevailing-wage work, stored-material documentation and COIs so the GC releases payment on time
current_process: Prepare SOV percentages in Excel or accounting software, collect lower-tier lien waivers, generate certified payroll in a separate payroll tool or LCPtracker, upload everything to the GC's portal (Procore Pay, GCPay, Textura, Built), then wait for the GC's compliance review
what_fails: Pay apps are rejected for arithmetic errors, overstated percent-complete, missing or unsigned lien waivers, no stored-materials documentation, or missing certified payroll; GC compliance holds delay submission; end-of-month crunch when a dozen subs submit inside a 48-hour window; each GC uses a different portal and waiver form
failure_frequency: Monthly per project per sub; a vendor guide (2026) estimates 35-50% of lien waivers require chasing under manual processes (vendor estimate, not independent)
cost_of_failure: Payment delayed by a billing cycle (30+ days) per rejection; admin time re-submitting; financing cost of carrying payroll and materials; specific 2026 days-to-pay statistics were not captured
existing_workaround: Dedicated billing/compliance staff; subscriptions to Siteline, Levelset, LienDone; templates per GC; calling the GC's PM to clear compliance holds
who_pays_today: Subcontractors pay billing software and staff time plus financing cost; GCs pay portal vendors (GCPay, Procore Pay, Textura) and AP staff

sources.note: March 2026 user review complains that compliance issues hold up pay app submission while waiting on the GC to clear them.
2026 reconciliation guide describing certified-payroll checks, end-of-month 48-hour submission crunch, and 35-50% lien waiver chase rate (vendor estimate).
Lists common pay-app rejection reasons: arithmetic errors, overstated percent-complete, missing/unsigned lien waivers, stored materials, missing certified payroll.
Vendor roundup showing the crowded sub-billing tool market (Siteline, GCPay, Procore Pay, Built, Trimble Pay).
Describes AP-side burden of pay apps, lien waivers and COIs.

firsthand_evidence: A GCPay user review from March 2026 says compliance issues cause delays in submitting pay apps while waiting on the GC to clear them. No r/Construction thread was captured; the planned Reddit and certified-payroll searches were blocked by the search budget.
key_unknowns: Primary statistic on average days-to-pay for subs in 2026 (Rabbet/Levelset surveys not retrieved); rejection rate of pay apps; how many small subs still bill from Excel; which pain is sharper, lien waivers or certified payroll.
technical_unlock: Document extraction over SOV spreadsheets, waiver PDFs and WH-347 forms can pre-check a pay-app package against each GC's rules before submission; Playwright-driven portal submission is feasible for a solo developer.
why_now: Davis-Bacon wage-determination changes and more prevailing-wage work under 2021-2024 federal infrastructure spending increased certified-payroll volume at small subs (inferred, not sourced in this run).
existing_solutions: Siteline, Levelset (Procore), LienDone, GCPay, Textura, Built, LCPtracker, eMars, Points North

title: Small defense machine shops pay $20k-$60k+ in year-one consulting to stand up ITAR programs and risk lapsed DDTC registration
affected_user: Owner of a 5-50 person contract manufacturer (machining, fabrication, electronics) taking on ITAR-controlled parts for primes
job_to_be_done: Register with DDTC (DS-2032), control technical data (drawings, CAD) so only US persons access it, screen employees and visitors, maintain records, and renew registration annually so the prime will send work
current_process: Hire an ITAR consultant to write a compliance manual, train staff, segregate ITAR drawings in a separate file share or enclave, pay the DDTC registration fee each year, and layer DFARS 7012 cyber requirements on top
what_fails: Registration fee is the smallest cost ($3,000 Tier 1 effective Jan 2025 per consultant sources; a $500 small-business discount is claimed but was not confirmed against DDTC); consultant estimates put first-year cost at $20k-$60k for small suppliers and $50k-$150k for mid-sized programs, with one illustrative ongoing annual cost near $85k; lapsed registration can require paying back fees for the gap; shops must simultaneously meet CMMC/DFARS 7012, doubling the compliance workload
failure_frequency: Annual registration renewal; every new employee, visitor, and drawing transfer is a control event; no primary statistic found on violation or lapse rates among small shops
cost_of_failure: $20k-$60k year-one consulting (small supplier) plus fee and staff time; loss of prime work if not registered; civil penalties for violations (figures not retrieved)
existing_workaround: Consultants, templated compliance manuals, separate ITAR file servers or GCC High tenants, declining ITAR work entirely
who_pays_today: Shops pay DDTC fees, consultants (T Globe, itarconsultant.us and similar), MSPs for enclaves; primes absorb supplier-pool shrinkage

sources.note: Reports $3,000 Tier 1 DDTC fee effective Jan 2025 and an illustrative ~$85k/yr ongoing cost for a small firm.
Consultant estimates $20k-$60k year-one consulting for small/mid suppliers; $20k-$40k plus fee for 10-50 employee shops.
Estimates $50k-$150k for a full program at mid-sized contract manufacturers.
Shop-oriented blog on CMMC+ITAR for small machine shops; notes lapsed registration means paying back fees for the gap; claims C3PAO certification paused as of Sept 2026 (unverified).
Gives $2,250-$4,750 tiered fee range citing 22 CFR 122.3(a); conflicts with other sources, unconfirmed.
2026 guide noting DFARS 252.204-7012 cyber expectations stack on ITAR for fabrication shops.

firsthand_evidence: No shop-owner post captured; all sources are consultants or vendor blogs serving small shops, which is itself a signal that shops are paying for this but weak as direct evidence of pain.
key_unknowns: Official DDTC fee schedule and small-business discount; how many small shops decline ITAR work; actual enforcement/penalty exposure for small shops; overlap with CMMC spending (is this one budget or two).
technical_unlock: None obvious beyond documentation templating; the controlling costs are access-controlled infrastructure, screening and legal judgment.
why_now: DDTC fee increase effective Jan 2025; CMMC Phase I since Nov 2025 forces shops to address both regimes together.
existing_solutions: ITAR consultants, Thoropass, PreVeil/GCC High for technical data, Visual Compliance (Descartes) for screening

title: Small medical device makers must rewrite QSR-era quality documentation to ISO 13485-aligned QMSR after the Feb 2, 2026 switchover while inspections move to a new compliance program
affected_user: Quality/regulatory lead at a small (under ~50 employee) US medical device manufacturer or contract manufacturer that built its QMS on 21 CFR 820 QSR and never obtained ISO 13485 certification
job_to_be_done: Bring procedures, records, terminology (e.g. DHF/DMR vs. medical device file, risk management per ISO 14971) and training into line with QMSR before an FDA inspection under Compliance Program 7382.850
current_process: Gap-assess the existing QSR-based quality manual against ISO 13485:2016 clauses plus FDA-retained requirements, rewrite SOPs, retrain staff, often with a regulatory consultant or an eQMS vendor migration
what_fails: FDA stated the burden should be no greater than QSR compliance and projected >$500M/yr net industry savings, but guides note small firms needing to overhaul documentation are the exception and bear a larger share of cost; QSIT was retired Feb 2, 2026 so firms face an unfamiliar inspection approach; ISO certification does not substitute for FDA inspection, so small firms cannot simply buy a cert
failure_frequency: One-time transition for every FDA-registered device establishment (effective Feb 2, 2026), then ongoing per inspection
cost_of_failure: unknown; FDA final-rule economic analysis gives aggregate net savings, not per-small-firm cost; consultant/eQMS fees not quantified in captured sources
existing_workaround: Hire regulatory consultants; adopt eQMS platforms (Greenlight Guru, Qualio, etc.) that ship QMSR templates; pursue ISO 13485 certification as a proxy
who_pays_today: Small device makers pay consultants and eQMS subscriptions; FDA pays investigator retraining

sources.note: Reports QMSR took effect Feb 2, 2026 incorporating ISO 13485:2016 by reference; QSIT retired.
Final rule coverage; FDA estimated annualized net cost savings of more than $500 million industry-wide.
eQMS vendor explanation of QSR-to-QMSR changes; notes small firms needing documentation overhaul as the exception to FDA's low-burden expectation.
Consultancy guide stating small firms bear a larger share of transition cost (no dollar figures).
Describes inspection shift to Compliance Program 7382.850 and that ISO certification does not replace FDA inspection.

firsthand_evidence: None captured; all sources are vendor/consultant/association commentary.
key_unknowns: Per-firm transition cost for small device makers (FDA Federal Register economic analysis not retrieved); how many small firms lack ISO 13485 alignment; early 483 observation trends under the new compliance program; whether the pain is sharp enough to pay for anything beyond existing eQMS templates.
technical_unlock: LLM gap analysis of an existing quality manual against ISO 13485/QMSR clause map is straightforward, but existing eQMS vendors already ship this; differentiation unclear.
why_now: QMSR effective Feb 2, 2026; QSIT retired same day; first inspection cycle under the new program is happening now.
existing_solutions: Greenlight Guru, Qualio, MasterControl, Arena, ETQ, regulatory consultancies (The FDA Group, Patient Guard)
